phonemes.desc: Syllable with unaspirated bilabial stop [p], open front vowel [a], and Tone 1 (high level, ˥). Pinyin 'b' is unaspirated, unlike English 'b' in word-initial position.
Syllable with unaspirated velar stop [k], labio-velar glide [w], open vowel [a], and Tone 4 (falling, ˥˩). The 'u' after 'g' indicates labialization [kʷ].

pronunciation.approximation: BAH-GWAH — first syllable high and level, second syllable falling (high to low) like a command.

kin.label: Related terms
kin.form: 易經 Yìjīng (I Ching); 六十四卦 liùshísì guà (sixty-four hexagrams)

pronunciation.note: 八卦 (Bāguà) refers to the eight trigrams of the Yijing: 乾 qián, 坤 kūn, 震 zhèn, 巽 xùn, 坎 kǎn, 離 lí, 艮 gèn, and 兌 duì. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is bā (Tone 1) + guà (Tone 4), as recorded in the Unihan Database (kMandarin). For historical context, Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 八 as *pret (GSR 0281a) and 卦 as *[k]ʷre-s (GSR 0879s). The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Bāguà correctly shows the high level tone of 'eight' and the falling tone of 'trigram'.

domains.title: The Eight Trigrams
domains.subtitle: Yijing Cosmology and Divination
domains.lead:
Bāguà is the Chinese universe reduced to eight three-line figures. Each trigram — 乾 Qián, 坤 Kūn, 震 Zhèn, 巽 Xùn, 坎 Kǎn, 離 Lí, 艮 Gèn, 兌 Duì — stacks yin and yang lines in every possible combination of three, producing a complete symbolic alphabet for describing situations, forces, and transformations. From the trigrams come the sixty-four hexagrams of the Yijing, the oldest continuously used divination manual in the world.

Bāguà is not only a fortune-telling tool. It is a map of reality: directions, seasons, family roles, body parts, and moral qualities all attach to the eight figures.

cards.name: The Three Lines
cards.desc: A solid line is yang; a broken line is yin. Three lines yield 2³ = 8 trigrams, the elementary vocabulary of change.

cards.name: Heaven and Earth
cards.desc: Qián ☰, three solid lines, is heaven and creative power; Kūn ☷, three broken lines, is earth and receptive yielding.

cards.name: Cosmic Directions
cards.desc: The Later Heaven arrangement assigns each trigram to a direction, a season, and a domain of human life.

cards.name: Divination Method
cards.desc: Yarrow stalks, coins, and milfoil turn trigrams into hexagrams, turning a question into a reading of timing and transformation.

symbols.name: Qián ☰ (Heaven)
symbols.meaning: Creativity, strength, the father, the creative impulse

symbols.name: Kūn ☷ (Earth)
symbols.meaning: Receptivity, devotion, the mother, the power of bearing

symbols.name: Zhèn ☳ (Thunder)
symbols.meaning: Arousal, movement, the eldest son, sudden change

symbols.name: Xùn ☴ (Wind/Wood)
symbols.meaning: Gentle penetration, the eldest daughter, influence

symbols.name: Kǎn ☵ (Water)
symbols.meaning: The abyss, danger, the middle son, the testing flow

symbols.name: Lí ☲ (Fire)
symbols.meaning: Clarity, attachment, the middle daughter, brightness

symbols.name: Gèn ☶ (Mountain)
symbols.meaning: Stillness, keeping still, the youngest son, boundary

symbols.name: Duì ☱ (Lake)
symbols.meaning: Joy, openness, the youngest daughter, completion

mythology.lead: The Bāguà are surrounded by origin stories that credit culture heroes and sages with their discovery. Fuxi reads the patterns of the world; King Wen elaborates the Changes in a Shang prison; the sages of the Xici invent the book as they invented writing and agriculture — in answer to human need. Whether history, legend, or mythic shorthand, the stories agree on one thing: the eight trigrams are a key to cosmic order, perfected at great cost.

myths.title: Fuxi Reads the Patterns of the World
myths.text: The oldest account of the trigrams' invention is not a story about a river monster but a sentence in the Xici zhuan (Appended Statements II): 'In ancient times, when Bao Xi (Fuxi) ruled the world, he looked up and contemplated the patterns of heaven, looked down and contemplated the patterns of earth; he observed the markings of birds and beasts and the adaptations of the land. Near at hand he took patterns from his own body, far off he took them from things — and so he created the eight trigrams to communicate with the virtue of the gods and to categorize the feelings of all things.' Later legend embroidered the contemplation into a marvel: a dragon-horse emerged from the Yellow River bearing the Hétú chart, and a divine turtle from the Luo bore the Luoshu writing, and from these the sage read the trigrams. The tradition itself (Xici I) preserves the kernel: 'The river produced the chart, the Luo produced the document; the sage modelled himself on them.' Either way, the claim is identical: the trigrams were not invented but noticed — the cosmos already written, waiting only to be read.

myths.title: King Wen Elaborates the Changes in Prison
myths.text: When King Wen of Zhou was imprisoned by the tyrant Zhòu of Shang — the tradition recorded by Sima Qian — he did not plot escape but divination: 'King Wen was imprisoned and elaborated the Zhōuyì' (Shiji 130). In captivity he doubled the eight trigrams into sixty-four hexagrams and wrote a statement for each, a one-line oracle distilled from the history and ethics of a people living under an oppressive dynasty. His son, the Duke of Zhou, is credited with the line statements, the judgements within each hexagram; Confucius or his school, centuries later, added the Ten Wings, turning a manual of milfoil divination into a philosophy of change. Sima Qian's sentence has carried enormous weight: it makes the Yijing literally a prison book, written by a condemned man mapping the one freedom no cell can close — the freedom to read the moment. The sequence of authorship — king, duke, sage — also quietly encodes the book's social range: ruler, minister, teacher.

myths.title: The Sage Who Invents According to Need
myths.text: The Xici appendix imagines human technology not as a fall but as a series of sages answering crises. When rule by knotted cords became inadequate, a later sage replaced them with written characters; before that, another sage taught agriculture when birds and beasts dwindled under bad kings. In the same passage, the author explains the Yijing's purpose: the sages made the eight trigrams and 'exposed the auspicious and inauspicious in them,' so that the people could meet each situation as it arose. Change (yi) is the one constant; the book exists because human beings need a grammar for situations that have never occurred before. This is why the Yijing never gives straight predictions — it gives structures for reflection. The myth of sage-invention dignifies the diviner: to consult the book is to join a long chain of sage problem-solvers, from Fuxi, who fished and hunted, through Shennong, who sowed, to King Wen, who suffered and saw.

myths.title: The Bagua Mirror Guards the Door
myths.text: In Chinese popular religion the eight trigrams descend from the scholar's desk to the lintel. The bāguà jìng — an octagonal mirror ringed with the trigrams around a taiji emblem at its centre — is hung above doorways across China and the diaspora to deflect harmful qi. A flat mirror confronts what comes straight; a concave mirror gathers and neutralizes; a convex mirror scatters 'poison arrows' from rooflines, sharp corners, and aggressive neighbours. Priests of the Daoist liturgical tradition also deploy the trigrams spatially: ritual registers assign each trigram a direction and a gate, and the complete octagonal arrangement claims the whole of space and time in a single emblem. The practice compresses the entire cosmology into household hardware — heaven, earth, thunder, wind, water, fire, mountain, and lake standing sentinel over a family's doorway. Whatever else it does, the mirror announces that the cosmos has a shape, and that a household can align itself with it.

lore.syncretism: Bāguà is shared by Confucian, Daoist, and folk-religious traditions, each giving the trigrams a different emphasis. Confucians read them as moral archetypes; Daoists use them in talismans and internal alchemy; feng shui masters arrange buildings by their directions. The arrangement called the Early Heaven sequence is associated with Fuxi and cosmogony, while the Later Heaven sequence is associated with King Wen and the flow of time. In Korea, the trigrams appear on the national flag; in Japan, they influenced Onmyōdō cosmology. Richard Wilhelm's 1923 German translation, rendered into English by Cary Baynes, introduced the I Ching to modern Europe and America, where it became a countercultural classic.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Bāguà are everywhere once you know how to look. The Korean flag places four of the trigrams at its corners; martial artists practice Baguazhang, the Eight Trigram Palm, walking in circles that map the directions; computer scientists and designers use the Unicode trigram block (U+2630–U+2637) as glyphs for menus and progress indicators. Feng shui consultants still lay the octagonal bagua over floor plans to diagnose relationships, wealth, career, and health. The I Ching itself has been translated into dozens of languages and consulted by everyone from Carl Jung to John Cage. The trigrams have proved durable because they are not answers; they are a grammar for asking better questions about change.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Bāguà is the intuition that reality can be modeled without being exhausted. Eight figures, each only three lines long, are enough to describe marriages, wars, harvests, illnesses, and revolutions because the trigrams do not describe events; they describe tendencies. A trigram is a weather pattern, not a weather report.

To consult the Yijing is to accept that you already know the answer but cannot yet see its shape. The trigram does not predict the future like a calendar; it clarifies the present like a mirror. In this sense Bāguà is less occult than psychological: it forces the questioner to recognize which forces are active, which are latent, and which direction the situation is turning. The eight figures are not magic. They are a discipline of attention.

lore.archaeology: The Bāguà are rooted in the Shang dynasty practice of pyromancy on oracle bones and turtle plastrons, though the trigram system itself reaches written maturity in the Zhou period. The oldest Yijing manuscripts include the Mawangdui silk Zhouyi (c. 168 BCE) and the Warring States bamboo slips from Guodian and Shanghai Museum collections. Han dynasty commentaries, including the Xici, fixed the philosophical interpretation of the trigrams, while Song and Ming editions transmitted the diagrams that remain standard today.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 八卦; traditional and simplified forms are identical. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Bāguà (Tone 1 + Tone 4). Bā means 'eight' and guà means 'trigram' or 'hexagram' in divinatory usage. The registrable form uses tone-marked Pinyin so the domain remains readable across scripts; the characters are displayed in the Original Script card. Baxter & Sagart reconstruct 八 as *pret and 卦 as *[k]ʷre-s.
